summary.title: Alexander Ross, Virgilii Evangelisantis Christiados libri XIII (Rotterdam: Arnold Leers, 1653) — the gospel narrative told in the words of Virgil, with the poet's own marginal source-tags.

prose.la: VIRGILII EVANGELISANTIS CHRISTIADOS LIBRI XIII. Inflante ALEXANDRO ROSÆO. Roterodami, Sumptibus Arnoldi Leers. 1653.
prose.en: The Christiad of Virgil Evangelizing, in Thirteen Books. With Alexander Ross blowing [the pipe]. Rotterdam, at the expense of Arnold Leers, 1653.

prose.la: VIRGILII EVANGELISANTIS CHRISTIADOS LIBRI XIII. In quibus omnia quæ de Domino nostro JESU CHRISTO in utroque Testamento, vel dicta, vel prædicta sunt, altisona Divini Maronis tubâ suavissimè decantantur.
prose.en: THE CHRISTIAD OF VIRGIL EVANGELIZING, IN THIRTEEN BOOKS. In which all that has been said or foretold of our Lord Jesus Christ in either Testament is most sweetly sung upon the resounding trumpet of the divine Maro.

prose.la: Inflante ALEXANDRO ROSÆO. Arma virumque Maro cecinit, nos acta Deumque; Cedant arma Viri, dum loquor acta Dei. ROTERODAMI. Ex Officinâ ARNOLDI LEERS, 1653.
prose.en: [The trumpet] blown by ALEXANDER ROSS. Maro sang of arms and the man; we sing of deeds and God. Let the arms of the man give way, while I recount the deeds of God. Rotterdam. From the workshop of Arnold Leers, 1653.

prose.la: Ad Illustrissimum Puerum CAROLUM Magnæ Britanniæ Principem. CAROLE, spes Patriæ, Patris justissima cura, Et generate Diis, & geniture Deos. Cui dextram HENRICI Magni, & caput opto JACOBI, Et pectus patrium religione sacrum. Vultus utrum præfert, præfer quoque moribus illum; Vtque refers patrem nomine, mente refer. Et facito mox cùm matura adoleverit ætas, Vt firmes Solymæ mœnia quassa tuæ. Mœnia quæ malesana cohors, inimica quieti, Tentat sacrilega præcipitare manu. Et CHRISTVM venerare, suo qui sanguine nobis Hanc Patriam peperit, totque trophæa tulit, Hostibus ejectis, & de Babylone triumphans; Quæ tibi grandiloquo concinit ore Maro. Hic vatum Princeps te Principe dignus habetur, Castaliæ hic fontes cum pietate bibes.
prose.en: To the Most Illustrious Boy CHARLES, Prince of Great Britain. CHARLES, hope of your country, your father's most rightful care, born of gods and destined to beget gods: for you I wish the right hand of Henry the Great, the head of James, and your father's heart, hallowed by religion. Whichever of the two your face displays, display him also in your character; and, as you reproduce your father in name, reproduce him in mind. And see to it, as soon as your years have ripened, that you strengthen the battered walls of your Jerusalem: walls which a frenzied band, hostile to peace, attempts to cast down with sacrilegious hand. Revere also Christ, who by his own blood won this fatherland for us and carried off so many trophies, having driven out his enemies and triumphed over Babylon: these deeds Maro sings to you in a grandiloquent voice. Here the prince of poets is accounted worthy of you, a prince; here you will drink from Castalia's springs together with piety.

prose.la: Hic simul Heroum laudes, & facta parentum, Et quid sit virtus intemerata, leges. Disce puer virtutem ex his, verumque laborem, Vt possis sceptro subdere Regna tuo. Quisquis sanctorum sequitur vestigia Patrum, Hic merito Patriæ dicitur esse Pater. C. T. V. studiosissimus ALEX. ROS.
prose.en:
Here too you will read the praises of heroes and the deeds of your forebears, and what unblemished virtue is. Learn virtue, boy, from these, and true toil, that you may be able to bring kingdoms under your sceptre. Whoever follows the footsteps of the holy Fathers is rightly said to be the Father of his country.

Your Highness's most devoted servant, ALEXANDER ROSS.

prose.la: Præfatio omnibus hoc Carmen lecturis utilis. HEM tibi, Amice Lector, Opus antelucanum, à me, horis hyemalibus matutinis nondum stratis egresso, decantatum; Aurora namque Musis amica, & reliquum diei annique tempus aliis studiis & negotiis impendere soleo. Sub gallicinium Cynthius (cui Gallus sacer est) aurem vellere & admonere solet, ut sub id tempus Dominum meum, cum Petro; quem ille voce tantum ter, ego verò vita & moribus sæpius abnegavi, cantando flerem, & flendo canerem; hanc Provinciam detractare, mihi religio fuit, præsertim Musarum ostiis apertis, & non invita Minerva; Eundem honorem exhibere Christo volenti, quem Homerus Vlyssi & Achilli, Virgilius Æneæ: ad hoc Opus concinnandum linguam
prose.en:
A Preface Useful to All Who Will Read This Poem.

Here for you, dear reader, is a work composed before dawn, sung by me during the winter morning hours before I had yet left my bed; for Dawn is friendly to the Muses, and I am accustomed to devote the remaining time of the day and year to other studies and business. At cockcrow Cynthius (to whom the cock is sacred) is wont to tug at my ear and urge me, at that hour, to weep with Peter for my Lord while singing, and to sing while weeping—my Lord whom Peter denied only three times in word, but whom I have denied more often in life and conduct. I scrupled to refuse this commission, especially with the doors of the Muses open and Minerva not unwilling. Wishing to render to Christ the same honor that Homer rendered to Ulysses and Achilles, and Virgil to Aeneas, for the composition of this work I chose the language…

prose.la: elegi Latinam, dicendi genus poeticum, & phrasin in Virgilianam: linguam praetuli Latinam, utpote omnium suavissimam, tanto aliis linguis elegantia superiorem, quanto olim fuit urbs urbibus eminentior; est etiam lingua communis maxime, & cujus beneficio religionis, civilitatis, legum, morum, disciplinarum, & artium participes sumus; dicendi autem genus elegi poëticum; utpote oratorio pręstantius; hujus enim finis sola est utilitas, illius verò utilitas voluptate conjuncta, & prodesse volunt & delectare Poetae, propterea omne tulit punctum: Deinde, Orator quivis esse potest, Poeta autem nemo, nisi cui à natura speciali quodam privilegio concessum est; nascimur enim Poetae, fimus Oratores: Tertio, efficacia in movendis affectibus longe Oratorem superat Poëta. Quis enim Orator Poëtam æquiparabit in describenda amoris, fortitudinis, doloris, aliarumque aut virtu¬
prose.en: …the Latin tongue, the poetic kind of speech, and Virgilian phrasing. I preferred the Latin tongue as the sweetest of all, and as far superior to other tongues in elegance as the City was once more eminent than other cities; it is besides the most widely shared language, and it is by its good offices that we have our part in religion, civility, laws, manners, the disciplines and the arts. The poetic kind of speech I chose as being more excellent than the oratorical; for the end of oratory is usefulness alone, whereas that of poetry is usefulness joined with pleasure, and poets aim both to profit and to delight, and on that account the poet has carried every vote. Next, anyone at all can be an orator, but no one can be a poet unless nature has granted it to him by some special privilege: poets we are born, orators we are made. Thirdly, in effectiveness at moving the affections the poet far surpasses the orator. For what orator will match a poet in setting out the force of love, of courage, of grief, and of the other virtues…

prose.la: tum aut passionum vi, nisi Poëtae partes agat, ut saepe Oratores factitare solent. Hinc Poësis à Platone, Aristotele, Plutarcho, aliisque viris sapientibus tantum laudata: hinc Imperatores, Principes, Philosophi, Theologi, Poëtices studium non solum in summo honore habuerunt, sed ipsi quoque in eodem egregiam operam navarunt; Alexander mortuum Homerum, vivo Aristoteli prætulit; pluris apud Heronem Syracusanum fuit Poëta Pindarus, quam Plato Philosophus : Virgilio carmina sua in theatro recitanti, universus populus Romanus perinde ac Imperatori assurrexit; ejusdem diem natalem quotannis celebravit Augustus; Ovidio Getarum gens barbara, splendidum sepulchrum extruxit; soli Poetae digni habiti sunt, qui cum Imperatoribus lauro coronentur; Plato Poëtas ἐρμουνέας & ὑπερέτας Deorum vocat; (in Jone,) Philosophia quæ in formandis moribus versatur, in Poetarum sententiis omnino radices egit;
prose.en: …or by the force of the passions, unless he plays the poet's part, as orators have often been in the habit of doing? Hence poetry has been so greatly praised by Plato, by Aristotle, by Plutarch, and by other wise men; hence emperors, princes, philosophers and theologians have not only held the study of poetry in the highest honour, but have themselves also spent excellent labour upon it. Alexander preferred Homer dead to Aristotle alive; with Hiero of Syracuse the poet Pindar counted for more than the philosopher Plato; when Virgil recited his verses in the theatre, the whole Roman people rose to its feet before him just as it would before the emperor; Augustus kept Virgil's birthday every year; the barbarous nation of the Getae raised a splendid tomb for Ovid; poets alone have been thought worthy to be crowned with laurel alongside emperors; Plato (in the Ion) calls poets the interpreters and the servants of the gods; and the philosophy which is concerned with the shaping of manners has struck its roots wholly in the sayings of the poets.

prose.la: (Sextus Empiricus l. cont. Mathem. c. 17.) Cùm pater meus daret operam, ut in bonum virum evaderem, omnia Homeri Carmina ediscere coegit, inquit Xenophon sub Niceratis persona. (in Symposio) Philosophari intendentibus non sunt Poemata defugienda, sed in poematibus naviter philosophandum. (Plutarc. de audiend. Poët.) Omnis aetas per poeticam longè perfectius fingitur, quam per exempla Philosophorum: idem quoque ibidem ostendit, civitatum & legislatorum fuisse vetus institutum, fabulas adhibere Poetarum, ad hominum mentes suaviter efficaciterq; movendas. Res sacra Poeta est. neque canere prius potest, quam, Deo * plenus : hinc θεόπνευσοι vates, Poetæ ποφου τὸ πριῆιν, vocantur; est enim Poeta, quasi alter Deus; non solum formam ut natura facit, introducens, sed ipsam quoque materiam sibi creans. Sane Poetæ Philosophorum parentes sunt; & exemplis idem (sed efficacius) docentes, quod illi prae-
prose.en: (Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians, ch. 17.) 'When my father was striving to make me turn out a good man, he compelled me to learn all the poems of Homer by heart,' says Xenophon in the person of Niceratus (in the Symposium). Those intending to philosophize must not flee from poems, but must philosophize vigorously within poems (Plutarch, On Listening to the Poets). Every age is shaped far more perfectly through poetry than through the examples of philosophers: in the same work he also shows that it was an ancient practice of states and lawgivers to employ the fables of poets to move human minds pleasantly and effectively. The poet is a sacred being, and cannot sing until he is filled with God *; hence bards are called θεόπνευστοι, 'god-breathed,' and poets take their name from τὸ ποιεῖν, 'to make.' For the poet is like a second God, not only introducing form as nature does, but also creating the very matter for himself. Indeed, poets are the parents of philosophers, teaching through examples—and more effectively—the same things that the latter teach through pre—

prose.la: ceptis. Longum autem, ut inquit Seneca, iter per praecepta, breve & efficax per exempla. Si autem in hoc ἀμέσω saeculo nobilissimum hoc studium pluris haberetur, minus esset rixarum, & infrugiferarum disputationum, quibus Ecclesiae Christianae tranquillitas toties turbatur; Quod verò ad phrases attinet, elegi Virgilianam, nihil enim illa purius, castius, ornatius; est enim Maro, non solum omnium Poetarum doctissimus, sed modestissimus quoque, & vere virgineus, in cujus divino opere non est ulla vox obscoena; in illo sententiae, numeri, figurae, simplicitas, candor, ornatus, incomparabilia, ut verbis utar * Scaligeri. Quantum sit in eo eruditionis reconditae, docti norunt commentatores; in eo, nec Ethica, nec Politica, nec Oeconomica, nec Astronomica, nec Geographica, nec Theologica desiderantur; ex eo gentium mores, terrarum, ac marium situs, bellorum stratagemata, militare robur, facundiae vires, deorum sa¬
prose.en: —cepts. The road, as Seneca says, is long through precepts, but short and effective through examples. If in this uncultured age this most noble study were more highly valued, there would be fewer quarrels and fruitless disputes by which the tranquillity of the Christian Church is so often disturbed. As for phrasing, I chose Virgilian style, for nothing is purer, more chaste, or more ornate; Maro is not only the most learned of all poets but also the most modest and truly maiden-like, in whose divine work there is no obscene word; in him the sentiments, rhythms, figures, simplicity, brilliance, and ornamentation are, to use the words of Scaliger, incomparable. How much recondite learning there is in him the learned commentators know; in him neither Ethics, nor Politics, nor Economics, nor Astronomy, nor Geography, nor Theology is lacking; from him [one learns] the customs of nations, the lay of lands and seas, the stratagems of wars, military strength, the powers of eloquence, the gods' sa—

prose.la: cra ediscuntur: est revera Virgilius omnis eruditionis promptuarium; Spero autem Opus hoc viris doctis & sapientibus non ingratum fore ; Sciolis autem & μινσομοσοις non canit meus Virgilius; ut nec olim Caligulæ; Scio enim esse quosdam adeò stupido & bruto ingenio, ut quibus Divinum Poëtices studium non magis sapiat quam Asinis lyra, aut Suibus amaracus. Sed hos ne in hominum quidem censu reponendos, cum * Scaligero puto: quidam forte stomachabuntur quod prophani Poëtae verbis & phra sibus religionis nostrae mysteria descripserini; quibus respondeo verbis D. Ambrosii: Cùm in fide nihil quod vituperare possunt invenerint, aliquid in sermone reprehendunt; agnoscunt non solum sententias, sed etiam versiculos Poetarum scripturis insertos divinis; unde gigantes, & vallem Ti* 11ieren. tanum Prophetici sermonis series non Damase de refugit, & Esaias Sirenas, &c. dixit: Hæc * Ambrosius, * Hieronymus, quam-
prose.en: sacred things are learned by heart; Virgil is truly a storehouse of all learning. I hope, moreover, that this work will not be unwelcome to learned and wise men. But my Virgil does not sing for smatterers and haters of the Muses, any more than he did for Caligula of old. For I know that some are of such dull and brutish disposition that the divine study of poetry has no more savour for them than a lyre has for asses or marjoram for swine. But I think, with Scaliger, that such men should not even be numbered among human beings. Some may perhaps take offence because I have described the mysteries of our religion in the words and phrases of a profane poet. To them I reply in the words of St Ambrose: "When they can find nothing in the faith to blame, they find fault with something in its language; they recognise not only the thoughts of the poets, but even their lines inserted into the divine Scriptures. Hence the course of prophetic discourse does not shrink from giants and the valley of the Titans, and Isaiah spoke of Sirens, and so forth" (On the Faith 3.1). Thus Ambrose. Jerome (Letter to Damasus, On the Prodigal Son), although—

prose.la: vis alioqui Poëtarum & Philosophorum nimis rigidus censor, concedit. Tamen, ut si quid in aliis utile reperimus, ad nostrum dogma convertamus; si quid verò superfluum de idolis, haec radamus, his calvitium inducamus, haec in unguium morem ferro desecemus; ut Israëlitæ jussi sunt tractare captivam mulierem. Non propter superstitionem prophanorum debemus Musicam fugere, aut literas non discere, quia earum repertorem dicunt esse Mercurium, inquit * D. Augustinus. Liceat ergo mihi cum Hebræis sacrum hoc tabernaculum immundorum animalium pellibus convestire, & cum primis Christianis Christum in idololatrico templo colere, illique aedem profanam consecrare; quamvis non video, quare tam castum & utile Virgilii poëma profanum dici debeat; imo illi potius profani sunt, qui, licet Christiani, impudici amoris illecebras carminibus immodestis doceant. Paulus nihil suae sanctimoniae
prose.en: —though otherwise too strict a critic of poets and philosophers, concedes this. 'Nevertheless, if we find anything useful in others, let us convert it to our own teaching; if anything superfluous about idols, let us shave it off, let us make it bald, let us cut it away with iron like fingernails, as the Israelites were commanded to treat a captive woman.' 'We should not flee from music on account of the superstition of the pagans, nor refrain from learning letters because they say Mercury was their inventor,' says St Augustine. Let me therefore be permitted, like the Hebrews, to cover this holy tabernacle with the skins of unclean animals, and, like the earliest Christians, to worship Christ in an idolatrous temple and consecrate a profane building to him—although I do not see why so chaste and useful a poem as Virgil's ought to be called profane; rather, those people are themselves profane who, though Christians, teach the enticements of unchaste love in immodest verses. Paul [lost] nothing of his holiness—

prose.la: amisit, quando vectus fuit in nave idololatrica Castoris & Pollucis; nec Christi nomen profanatur, si in nave Virgiliana vehatur : sed quis audet dicere Maronem, de Christo nullam habuine cognitionem, cùm de eo tam apertè scribat in 4 Ecloga, & in digressu de morte Caesaris, in fine 1 Geor. nemo tam coecus est, quin haec de Christo esse dicta, perspiciat, inquit L. Vives. Sed cur non boni illi viri, qui omnium mortalium purissimi haberi volunt, & qui nisi quod ipsi faciunt, nil rectum putant; cur, inquam, non succensent Apostolis, qui linguis profanarum Gentium Christianam Religionem, & Scripturas per Orbem propagarunt? Quod autem nomina Deorum Gentilium hic usurpamus, sciant nobis tam fas esse vocabula à profano usu ad sacrum transferre, quam olim fuit Hebraeis, ex profana Aegyptiorum supellectile Tabernaculi vasa, & ornamenta con-
prose.en: —when he sailed in the idolatrous ship of Castor and Pollux; nor is the name of Christ profaned if it is carried in the Virgilian vessel. But who dares say that Maro had no knowledge of Christ, when he writes of him so openly in the Fourth Eclogue and in the digression on the death of Caesar at the end of Georgics 1? 'No one is so blind as not to see that these things were said about Christ,' says Ludovico Vives. But why do those fine fellows—who wish to be regarded as the purest of all mortals and who think nothing right except what they themselves do—why, I ask, do they not reproach the Apostles, who propagated the Christian religion and the Scriptures throughout the world in the languages of profane nations? As for our use here of the names of the pagan gods, let them know that it is as lawful for us to transfer words from profane use to sacred as it once was for the Hebrews to fashion the vessels and ornaments of the Tabernacle from the profane furnishings of the Egyptians—

prose.la: flare. Porphyrium male habuit, quod * Origenes omnes Graecorum divitias ad locupletandam Christianam doctrinam contulit. Moyses Disciplinas Aegyptiorum, Daniel Sapientiam Chaldaeorum, & D. Paulus Poetas didicerunt, ut his religionem locupletiorem redderent: quanto Auro, Argento, & veste suffarcinatus, exivit de Aegypto Cyprianus, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, Hilarius, hoc prior Moyses fecerat eruditus omni sapientia Aegyptiorum, inquit Augustinus. Præterea illi nobis verborum sunt Authores, eodem a 40. Augustino teste. Non mirum Julianum Christianis humanarum literarum studiis interdixisse, cùm animadvertisset Ethnicos propriis suis pennis à Christianis configi. Ergo mihi liceat bist. c. 10. Virgiliani Carminis supellectilem pretiosam (quamvis profanam ex illorum Senatusconsulto) ad meliorem usum transferre, & Religionis nostrae gemmam aureo illo annulo includere. Deinde, nomina haec Deorum à
prose.en: Porphyry was vexed that Origen brought all the riches of the Greeks to enrich Christian doctrine. Moses learned the disciplines of the Egyptians, Daniel the wisdom of the Chaldaeans, and St Paul the poets, so as to make religion richer by their means: 'laden with how much gold, silver, and raiment did Cyprian, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary come out of Egypt! Before them Moses had done the same, learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,' says Augustine. Moreover, they are the originators of our very words, as the same Augustine attests. It is no wonder that Julian forbade Christians the study of humane letters, when he had perceived that the pagans were being transfixed with their own feathers by Christians. Therefore let me be permitted to transfer the precious furnishings of Virgilian song—profane though they be by the decree of those senators—to a better use, and to set the jewel of our religion in that golden ring. Furthermore, these names of the gods were—

prose.la: nobis furto ablata sunt. Quis enim Poëtarum, quis Sophistarum, qui non omnino de Prophetarum fonte pota"Avaverit? teste * Tertulliano. Quis nescit nomen Jovis, à Jehova deductum? & Adonis ab Adonai, & Jacchi à Jah, & Vulcani à Tubal Cain, & Musæi à Moyse, & Jani, quo Noachum intelligo, à Jain, Vino; ergo liceat nobis quod nostrum est vindicare, & à possessoribus illis injustis eripere. Tertio: nomine Jovis non intelligebant Poctæ Idolum aliquod, sed verum & supremum Deum; ut ex Virgilianis Epithetis constat; est enim illi Jupiter, hominum rerumque repertor; divûm Pater, atque hominum Rex, qui cœlum tempestatesque serenat; rerum cui summa potestas; qui foedera fulmine sancit; qui nutu tremefacit Olympum; Superi Regnator Olympi: Pater omnipotens, qui res hominumque Deumque, aeternis regit Imperiis; torquet qui Sidera Mundi, Rex Ætheris alti: Scio non defuturos
prose.en: ...were stolen from us. For what poet, what sophist has not drunk at all from the fountain of the Prophets? Tertullian is witness. Who does not know that the name of Jove is derived from Jehovah, Adonis from Adonai, Iacchus from Jah, Vulcan from Tubal Cain, Musaeus from Moses, and Janus—by whom I mean Noah—from Jain, meaning wine? Let us therefore reclaim what is ours and wrest it from those unjust possessors. Thirdly, by the name of Jove the poets meant not any idol but the true and supreme God, as is evident from the Virgilian epithets. For in Virgil Jupiter is "the creator of men and things"; "father of the gods and king of men, who clears the sky and calms the storms"; "he who holds supreme power over all things"; "he who ratifies treaties with the thunderbolt"; "he who makes Olympus tremble with a nod"; "ruler of high Olympus"; "almighty Father, who governs the affairs of men and gods with eternal dominion"; "he who turns the stars of the world"; and "king of heaven on high." I know that there will be no lack of Momuses,

prose.la: Momos, qui hunc laborem nostrum tanquam inutilem carpent & damnabunt; sed non me latet facilius esse μωμᾶαξ, quàm μιμῆας, reprehendere, quam apprehendere; quis mortalium αμωμος est, & illi ridiculo Deo non obnoxius? sed tales aut Scioli sunt, aut Sycophantæ, aut Philautæ, qui vel ex ignorantia, vel malevolentia vel nimia sui opinione carpunt ea quae ipsi vel non intelligunt, vel praestare nequeunt. Certè à Judæ Proditoris mente non sunt alieni, qui me calumniabuntur, quod pretiosum hoc Unguentum, cum Magdalena, in Dominum meum effuderim; an mihi non licebit fertis laureis & floribus illius caput ornare, quod pro me spinis perforatum fuit? aut Templum chartaceum, illi fortè gratius Templo marmoreo, extruere, & dedicare, qui pro me sanctissimum corporis sui Templum dissolvit? Christum canere & laudare, est opus beatorum coelitum; est finis creationis & redemptionis
prose.en: Momuses, who will carp at this labor of ours as useless and condemn it; but I am well aware that it is easier to find fault than to imitate, to censure than to comprehend. What mortal is without fault and not exposed to that god of ridicule? Such men, however, are either smatterers, slanderers, or self-lovers: out of ignorance, malice, or excessive self-regard, they carp at things which they themselves either do not understand or are incapable of accomplishing. Certainly those who will vilify me because, with Magdalene, I have poured this precious ointment upon my Lord are not far removed from the disposition of Judas the Betrayer. Shall I not be permitted to adorn with laurel garlands and flowers the head that for my sake was pierced with thorns? Or to build and dedicate a paper temple—perhaps more pleasing to him than a marble temple—to him who for my sake dissolved the most holy temple of his own body? To sing of and praise Christ is the work of the blessed inhabitants of heaven; it is the purpose of our creation and redemption.

prose.la: nostrae, ergo mihi sit fas illius laudes hic pro modulo meo balbutire. Non est opus inutile juventutem Christianam, a lectione impudicorum Carminum, ad sacram Historiam, jam doctissimis expressam versibus retrahere. Fastidienti stomacho salubrem Scripturarum cibum, mihi liceat, sapientis Medici instar, suavi condimento gratiorem reddere. Hic enim cum pura Virgiliana phrases, veram pietatem, & Religionis nostrae mysteria à teneris annis imbibent. Plato docet, Legum-latores Poetis uti, ut juvenum animi Carminibus deliniti, legibus obsequantur, nec futurus est hic labor Theologis omnino sterilis; praeter enim Divinas Meditationes, sacram Historiam, & Religionis nostrae arcana, hic aptas similitudines, phrases, & figuras suavissimas, ad exornandas conciones invenient, omnibus sane hoc opus futurum est, & utile & jucundum, nisi qui sint, qui mallent generosum vinum ex vase fi-
prose.en: …of our redemption. Therefore, let it be lawful for me here to stammer out his praises according to my modest ability. It is no useless undertaking to draw Christian youth away from reading indecent poems and back to sacred history, now expressed in the most learned verse. Like a wise physician, let me make the wholesome food of the Scriptures more agreeable to a squeamish stomach by means of a pleasant seasoning. For here, together with pure Virgilian diction, they will imbibe true piety and the mysteries of our religion from their earliest years. Plato teaches (Laws 2) that lawgivers should employ poets, so that the minds of the young, charmed by songs, may obey the laws. Nor will this labour be altogether fruitless for theologians; for besides divine meditations, sacred history, and the mysteries of our religion, they will find here apt comparisons, turns of phrase, and most pleasing figures with which to embellish sermons. Indeed, this work will be both useful and delightful to everyone, unless there are some who would rather drink fine wine from an earthenware vessel than from a golden cup.

prose.la: ctili, quàm ex aureo poculo bibere. Nulla autem est in hoc Opere (exceptis paucis) linea, in qua non invenies integrum Virgilianum Carmen, vel saltem dimidium, aut phrases illius; more autem poëtico fictiones. quasdam, sed pias, & Religioni consonas immiscui, ne versifex tantum esse videar; quod autem Scriptura fictionibus delectetur, testantur tot parabolæ & Apologi per sacram paginam sparsi; ubi autem suspicabar scrupulum aliquem Lectorem malè habiturum, adjeci marginalem notam sensus mei interpretem: qui plures desiderat, consulat priorem editionem. Vale Lector, & his mecum fruere; tibique exopto tantam in legendo, quantam ego in fingendo voluptatem habui.
prose.en: …than to drink it from a golden cup. But in this work there is, with few exceptions, no line in which you will not find an entire Virgilian verse, or at least half a verse, or phrases of his. Moreover, after the manner of poets, I have intermingled certain fictions—pious ones, however, and consonant with religion—lest I should seem to be merely a versifier. That Scripture delights in fictions is attested by the many parables and fables scattered throughout the sacred page. Wherever, however, I suspected that some scruple might trouble the reader, I added a marginal note interpreting my meaning; whoever desires more such notes should consult the earlier edition. Farewell, reader, and enjoy these things with me; I wish you as much pleasure in reading as I had in inventing them.

prose.la: IN hoc Opere, in quo sacros Scriptores civitate donavi, & Virgilium ex Romano Christianum, & ex Advena feci Proselytam: Sub nomine Sionis & Solyma describitur Ecclesiae Christi status, ab initio mundi, usque ad Domini in coelos elevationem. Variè illam oppugnat & persequitur Rex Pluto seu Satan; qui nullum non movet lapidem, ut Regnum suum Ecclesia subversâ in terris stabiliat, sed frustra semper enim Christus viros virtute & miraculis praestantes praemisit, qui Solymam à Satanae malitia & conatibus tuerentur; Tandem ipse venit, qui doctrina, virtute, miraculis, & morte, Regnum Babylonum evertit; Ecclesiam stabilivit; de Plutone & malorum Spirituum conciliabulo triumphavit.
prose.en: In this Work, in which I have granted citizenship to the sacred Writers and made Virgil from a Roman into a Christian and from a stranger into a proselyte: Under the names of Sion and Solyma is described the state of the Church of Christ, from the beginning of the world to the Lord's ascension into heaven. King Pluto, or Satan, attacks and persecutes her in various ways; he leaves no stone unturned to establish his own kingdom on earth by overthrowing the Church, but always in vain, for Christ has always sent ahead men outstanding in virtue and miracles to defend Solyma from Satan's malice and schemes. At last he himself came, who by his teaching, virtue, miracles, and death overthrew the Kingdom of Babylon, established the Church, and triumphed over Pluto and the council of evil Spirits.

prose.la: Admonitio ad Lectorem. IN angustiore margine, l significat librum; E, Eclogam; G, Georgicorum librum; AE, Aeneadum: Ubi verò figura solitaria ponitur, absque adjectione alicujus literae, ibi liber Aeneados significatur.
prose.en: Notice to the Reader. In the narrower margin, L signifies a book; E, an Eclogue; G, a book of the Georgics; and AE, a book of the Aeneid. Wherever, however, a numeral is placed by itself, without the addition of any letter, a book of the Aeneid is meant.

prose.la: Pluto animadvertens Solymæ fundamenta ab Abelo jacta, invidia stimulat Cainum Babylonis fundatorem, ut fratrem (quod illius sacrificium Deo acceptum fuit) interimeret; quo occiso, Deus alios excitat qui Solymam ædificent, nempe Sethum, Enosh, Kenam, Malaleël, Iared, Henocum, qui ad Paradisum fuit raptus; Methusalem, Noachum, cujus temporibus, instigante Plutone, Sethi posteri matrimonia contrahunt cum filiabus Caini; ex quibus procreantur Gigantes, quorum sceleribus provocatus Deus diluvium immisit, quo homines pecudesque perierunt, exceptis paucis in Arca servatis; cùm autem Noachus ex columbâ intellexisset siccatam rursus terram, Arcâ egreditur, victimam offert: varia præcepta filiis dat, quos agriculturam docet; cum illis Deus fœdus pepigit; sed senex vino captus, à filio Cham deridetur: interea Pluto, ut rursus Solymæ ædificationem impediret, omnes ad extructionem turris Babel hortatur; quos Deus iratus dispersit, & loquelam confundit; Abramum ex Chaldæa ad extruendam Solymam evocat; illi Christus promittitur, & Canaan; Lothum captivum liberat. Describitur terra, bellum, & excidium Sodomitarum: quæ de Abele, Noacho, Abramo, &c. dicuntur, Christo applicantur.
prose.en: Pluto, observing that the foundations of Solyma had been laid by Abel, incites Cain, the founder of Babylon, through envy to kill his brother because Abel's sacrifice had been accepted by God. After Abel is killed, God raises up others to build Solyma, namely Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, who was carried off to Paradise, Methuselah, and Noah. In Noah's time, at Pluto's instigation, Seth's descendants marry the daughters of Cain; from them the Giants are begotten. Provoked by their crimes, God sends a flood in which human beings and beasts perish, except for the few preserved in the Ark. When Noah learns from the dove that the earth has become dry again, he leaves the Ark and offers a sacrifice. He gives his sons various commandments and teaches them agriculture; God makes a covenant with them. But the old man, overcome by wine, is mocked by his son Ham. Meanwhile Pluto, in order to hinder the building of Solyma once again, urges everyone to construct the tower of Babel; God angrily disperses them and confounds their speech. He summons Abram from Chaldaea to build Solyma; Christ and Canaan are promised to Abram, and Abram frees the captive Lot. The land, the war, and the destruction of the Sodomites are described. What is said about Abel, Noah, Abram, and the others is applied to Christ.

marginalia.text: Horrentia. & horrenda apud Virgilium significant veneranda saepe & timenda; sic horrenda Sibylla Ae.6. horrendum religione Ae. horrenda virgo, Ae.11. Christi autem opera Diabolo & impiis fuerunt vere horrenda.
marginalia.text_en: Horrentia. In Virgil horrentia and horrenda often signify things worthy of reverence and fear: thus "the awe-inspiring Sibyl," Aen. 6; "awe-inspiring through religious sanctity," Aen.; and "the awe-inspiring maiden," Aen. 11. Christ's works, however, were truly dreadful to the Devil and the wicked.
marginalia.explanation: He defends his own diction: horrenda in Virgil carries awe, not mere horror.

marginalia.text: profugus fuit sponte non coacte, pro nobis, non pro se.

marginalia.text: Alto, phrasi Hebraea, lacus enim apud eos Mare vocatur.

marginalia.text: Per Superos, Principes, Sacerdotes, Scribas, &c. intelligo.
marginalia.text_en: By "the gods above" I mean the rulers, the priests, the scribes, and the like.
marginalia.explanation: Keys Virgil's pagan machinery to the gospel's human authorities.

marginalia.text: Per Plutonem intelligo Diabolum, qui τὴν πλούτου δόσιν, divitiarum largitor videri vult, & talis creditur à cultoribus suis: vel quia divitiae è terrae visceribus, haud procul ab ejus regno eruuntur, vel διὰ τὸ πλουτεῖν τοῖς νεκροῖς, omnes enim mortuorum impiorum animae, ad eum descendunt.
marginalia.text_en: By Pluto I understand the Devil, who wishes to be seen as τὴν πλούτου δόσιν, the bestower of riches, and is believed to be such by his worshippers: either because riches are dug out of the bowels of the earth, not far from his kingdom, or διὰ τὸ πλουτεῖν τοῖς νεκροῖς, because he is rich in the dead; for all the souls of the wicked dead go down to him.
marginalia.explanation: Etymological gloss on Pluto's name, turning the classical god into Satan.

marginalia.text: Haec urbs quam Christus condidit, est caelestis Hierusalem, nempe Ecclesia, quae passim in hoc Opere Sion & Solyma vocatur, fecerunt civitates duas, Amores duo, &c. Aug. de Civitate Dei, lib.14. cap. ult. & lib.15. in exordio.
marginalia.text_en: This city which Christ founded is the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which throughout this work is called Sion and Solyma. Two loves made two cities, &c. Aug. de Civitate Dei, lib. 14. cap. ult. & lib. 15. in exordio.
marginalia.explanation: Names the epic's city: Aeneas's Rome becomes Augustine's City of God.

marginalia.text: Romam idololatricam evertit juxta vaticinium Sibillinum, ῥώμη μὲν ῥύμη ἔσται καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος, &c.
marginalia.text_en: He overthrew idolatrous Rome according to the Sibylline oracle, ρώμη μὲν ῥύμη ἔσεται καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος, &c.—Rome shall become a street, and Delos shall become obscure.
marginalia.explanation: The oracle turns on puns of Rhome/rhyme and Delos/adelos.

marginalia.text: Licet Deus sit mens seu anima mundi, non est tamen animal mundus, ut Platonici & Stoici volebant: est enim forma assistens, non informans, quia non est pars & substantia imperfecta.
marginalia.text_en: Although God is the mind or soul of the world, the world is nevertheless not an animal, as the Platonists and Stoics would have it: for he is an assisting form, not an informing one, since he is not a part of it, nor an imperfect substance.

marginalia.text: Per Parcas hic non intelligo vel ipsum Deum, vel inevitabilem necessitatem, vel tria tempora, praesens, praeteritum, & futurum, vel pariendi tempora, unde Nona, Decima, Morta, ut videre est in A. Gellio l.3. c.16. Arist. de mundo, Theod. &c. ad Graec. infid. ser.6. vel denique cum Poetis, Iovis scribas; sed Prophetas intelligo, Sp. Sancti amanuenses, qui notitiam rerum praeteritarum, praesentium, & futurarum habuerunt; qui nulli parcunt in denunciandis Dei judiciis: μοῖραι sunt, id est, sors & portio Domini; eadem significatione κλῆροι Sacerdotes vocantur.
marginalia.text_en: By the Fates I do not here understand God himself, nor inevitable necessity, nor the three times — present, past, and future — nor the seasons of childbirth, whence Nona, Decima, Morta, as may be seen in A. Gellius l. 3. c. 16., Aristotle de mundo, Theodoret &c. ad Graec. infid. ser. 6.; nor, finally, the scribes of Jove, as the poets have it. Rather I understand the Prophets, the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, who had knowledge of things past, present, and to come, and who spare no man in denouncing the judgments of God. They are μοῖραι, that is, the lot and portion of the Lord; in the same sense priests are called κλῆροι.
marginalia.explanation: He turns the Parcae into the Prophets, playing on parcere, to spare, and on moira as "portion."

marginalia.text: Diabolus Draco & Serpens vocatur: hac forma apparuit Evae: sub hac forma cultus apud Gentes. Aesculapio, Mercurio, Minervae consecratur Serpens: horti Hesperidum custos in locis sacris pingi solitus, inter sidera relatus: & quibus non honoribus cultus fuit Daemon sub forma & nomine serpentis, hinc dii gentium serpentinis pedibus picti.
marginalia.text_en: The Devil is called Dragon and Serpent: in this shape he appeared to Eve, and under this shape he was worshipped among the nations. The serpent is consecrated to Aesculapius, to Mercury, to Minerva; as guardian of the garden of the Hesperides it was regularly painted in holy places, and was set among the stars. With what honours was the demon not worshipped under the form and name of a serpent! Hence the gods of the nations are painted with serpents' feet.

prose.la: Mortuo Abrahamo, in filium Isaac Palæstinos concitat Pluto, qui invidia puteos ejus obturant pulvere, ut ab ædificatione Solymæ deterreant; sed Deus ei apparens promissa olim Abramo renovat, gemellos dat qui in utero matris luctando præsignabant dissidium quod inter ipsos, & eorum posteros futurum erat; nam Jacobum minorem odio assiduo insequutus est Esau, quare suasu matris Jacob ad Labanum se recipit, illique 26 annis inservit; Deus autem sæpius illum consolatur, promittitque Christum ex eo venturum, & Babylonem eversurum; ostendit illi scalam super qua Angeli ascendebant & descendebant; exercitus Angelicus ad illum tuendum mittitur; cum Christo sub forma Angeli luctatur, victorque evadit, sed poplite ab Angelo percusso claudicavit; & Pluto in magnum discrimen Jacobum & filios conjicit ob raptam Dinam Jacobi filiam; inde ut senem luctu necaret, omnes fratres in Josephum quem pater præ reliquis diligebat, concitat; in puteum puerum demittunt, Judas illum vendit, qui tandem magnus in aula Pharonis evasit ob somniorum interpretationem; pater conspecta tunica hædina sanguine tincta occisum credidit, quare diu Josephum luget; filios in Ægyptum frumentatum mittit, quos Joseph tandem in gratiam recepit. Pluto interea in Jobum sævit, cujus historia describitur; omniaque Christo applicantur.
prose.en: After Abraham's death, Pluto stirs up the Philistines against his son Isaac. Out of envy they stop up his wells with dust, so as to deter him from building Jerusalem; but God appears to him, renews the promises once made to Abraham, and gives him twins, who by struggling in their mother's womb foreshadowed the discord that was to arise between the brothers and between their descendants. For Esau pursued the younger twin, Jacob, with unremitting hatred; therefore, at his mother's urging, Jacob withdraws to Laban and serves him for twenty-six years. God, however, repeatedly comforts him and promises that Christ will descend from him and overthrow Babylon. He shows him a ladder upon which angels were ascending and descending; an angelic host is sent to protect him; he wrestles with Christ in the form of an angel and emerges victorious, but limps after the angel strikes him in the hollow of the knee. Pluto also casts Jacob and his sons into great danger because of the abduction of Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Then, in order to kill the old man through grief, he stirs up all the brothers against Joseph, whom his father loved above the others. They lower the boy into a pit; Judah sells him; and at last, because of his interpretation of dreams, he rises to greatness in Pharaoh's court. On seeing the kidskin coat stained with blood, his father believes him to have been killed and therefore mourns Joseph for a long time. He sends his sons into Egypt to obtain grain, and Joseph eventually receives them into his favor. Meanwhile Pluto rages against Job, whose story is related; and everything is applied to Christ.

marginalia.text: Teraphim intelligo quae surata est Rachel, Penates dicti sunt, quod in aedium penetralibus colebantur, vel quod per eos penitus spiramus, vivimus, intelligimus. Vocabantur etiam Dii magni; Apollo enim, Neptunus, Jupiter, Minerva, Juno, Vesta, &c. & Penates & Dii magni apud Poetas dicti sunt. Vide Macr. Sat. lib. 3. cap. 4. Nat. Com. lib. 4. c. 2. Servium, &c.
marginalia.text_en: By Teraphim I understand what Rachel stole. They were called Penates, because they were worshipped in the inner chambers (penetralia) of houses, or because through them we inwardly (penitus) breathe, live, and understand. They were also called the Great Gods; for Apollo, Neptune, Jupiter, Minerva, Juno, Vesta, etc. are called both Penates and Great Gods by the poets. See Macr. Sat. lib. 3. cap. 4. Nat. Com. lib. 4. c. 2. Servius, etc.
marginalia.explanation: He glosses Rachel's stolen teraphim by identifying them with the Roman Penates, so that Virgil's vocabulary will carry the Hebrew thing.

marginalia.text: Eumenides hic masculini generis facio, eadem licentia qua Virgilius Venerem & Alecto Deos vocat : Descendo ac ducente Deo, Aen. 2. Nec dextra erranti Deus abfuit, id est, Alecto. Aen.7. Scivit enim doctissimus Poeta, Venerem esse semen genitalis, quod est potentia, tam mas, quam foemina. Et cum Alecto sit spiritus malus, non decuit ille semper foemineo sexui alligari, licet hoc Poetae alii faciunt; forte quia maligni spiritus hunc Sexum saepius assumunt quam virilem: Aen. 3. sunt illis virginei vultus. Sic Aen. 7. Alecto in vultus sese transformat miles. & fit Calybe Junonis avis anus, &c. Hic autem per Eumenides intelligo Cacodaemones; ut enim illae, sic hi sunt Dei Ministri, &c. Scelerum vindices, malorum hominum tortores; noctis & tenebrarum filii: sunt etiam aeri-vagi : vocantur etiam angues & canes, in abysso habitant. Tisiphone a τίσις ultio, & Φόνος caedes, μεγαίρειν invidere, Ἄληκτος nunquam cessans, sunt nomini Diabolis aptissima, illi enim nunquam cessant ultione, & caedibus, & invidia, genus humanum infestare.
marginalia.text_en: Here I make the Eumenides masculine, with the same licence by which Virgil calls Venus and Allecto gods: "I descend, with a god leading," Aen. 2; "Nor was a god absent from the wandering right hand"—that is, Allecto—Aen. 7. For the most learned poet knew that Venus is the seed of generation, which is a power as much male as female. And since Allecto is an evil spirit, it was not fitting for him always to be bound to the female sex, although other poets do this—perhaps because evil spirits assume this sex more often than the male: Aen. 3, "They have maiden faces." Thus, in Aen. 7, Allecto transforms himself into the features of an old woman, and becomes Calybe, Juno's aged [priestess], etc. Here, however, by the Eumenides I mean evil demons; for as the former are, so the latter are ministers of God, avengers of crimes, tormentors of wicked men, sons of night and darkness. They also wander the air; they are also called serpents and dogs, and dwell in the abyss. Tisiphone, from τίσις, "vengeance," and φόνος, "slaughter"; [Megaera, from] μεγαίρειν, "to envy"; and Ἄληκτος, "never ceasing," are names most apt for devils, for they never cease to assail the human race with vengeance, slaughter, and envy.
marginalia.explanation: He justifies making the Furies male by Virgilian precedent, then converts them outright into demons.

marginalia.text: Adorare — whether from the word Ador, the grain destined for sacrifices; or from ores, “mouths” [sic] (hence "to adore the people" in Apuleius l. 2. is to address them); or from orare, as in Aen. 10., "I, Turnus, willingly entreat you," that is, I earnestly entreat you. It was performed in various ways: 1. by kissing one's own hand, Job. 21. 27.; 2. another's hand; 3. by bending the knee; 4. by stretching out the hands; 5. by veiling the head, and heads before the altars: "we are veiled with a Phrygian robe," Aen. 2.; 6. by sitting — so Pythagoras taught: let them sit when adoring; 7. by prostrating the body on the ground: thus the Persians adored their kings. In marriage, to adore one's wife is to kiss her, etc.
marginalia.text_en: Adorare—whether from the word Ador, grain destined for sacrifices; or from ore, "mouth" (hence in Apuleius, book 2, populum adorare means "to address the people"); or from orare, "to entreat," as in Aeneid 10: "I, Turnus, willingly entreat you," that is, "I earnestly entreat you." It was performed in various ways: 1. by kissing one's own hand, Job 21:27; 2. by kissing another's hand; 3. by bending the knee; 4. by extending the hands; 5. by veiling the head—and, before the altars, our heads: "we are veiled in Phrygian raiment," Aeneid 2; 6. by sitting—so Pythagoras taught: when worship is performed, let them sit; 7. by prostrating the body on the ground—thus the Persians worshipped their kings. In marriage, to adore one's wife is to kiss her, and so forth.

marginalia.text: Ausitis
marginalia.text_en: "From Abraham he was the fifth, a descendant of Esau." Athanas. in Synop. He was not, therefore, a Hebrew descended from Nahor, as the Hebrews and Jerome on Job would have it: for the land of Uz lies in Idumaea and on the borders of Arabia. Hence Job is called an Arab by Chrysostom. Job's three friends too were his neighbours, and Idumaeans. The land of Uz is called Ausitis by the Seventy. See August. l. 18. de civit. c. 47. Chrysost. Hom. 2. de patient. Job. Origen, Theodoret, etc.
marginalia.explanation: He rejects Jerome and the rabbinic line to make Job an Edomite Arab, not a Hebrew.

prose.la: Jacobo & Josepho mortuis, Satan ab Israëlitis alienat Pharonis animum, quibus gravia pensa imponit; sed Deus populi sui misertus, Moysen, ad Regem cum mandatis mittit, ut Solymæos ex servitute, variis editis signis & miraculis liberet; tandem Ægypto, multis cladibus affecta, Rege, dum Israëlitas insequitur, in mari submerso, Israëlitæ incolumes transeunt; qui instigante Plutone, in varia peccata incidunt, & in se Dei iram provocant. Lex promulgatur, Manna pluit, nubes interdiu, ignis noctu, viam per desertum monstrat, in quo ob peccata annos 40 errarunt: tria millia hominum ob idololatriam occisa; tabernaculum exstruitur, Pontificis indumenta describuntur. Core cum sociis murmurant & conspirant in Moysen; igniti serpentes mittuntur: Moyses in Pisgah moritur, populus duce Josua transit Jordanum. Describitur terra Chanaan, ubi varia bella inter Solymæos & terræ Incolas. Tandem Josua victor evasit, & Chananaeos subjugavit; cui vita functo, sequuti sunt Judices, qui Solymæam Plutonis invidia sæpe ab hostibus oppressum liberarunt. Gedeon stratagemate hostes in fugam conjicit. Jephthe victor domum rediens, filiam immolat. Describitur Ecclesiæ fœlicitas; & ad Christum fit omnium harum historiarum applicatio.
prose.en: With Jacob and Joseph dead, Satan turns Pharaoh's mind against the Israelites, upon whom Pharaoh imposes heavy tasks; but God, taking pity on his people, sends Moses to the king with his commands, so that by performing various signs and miracles he may free the people of Jerusalem from slavery. At last, after Egypt has been afflicted by many plagues and the king has drowned in the sea while pursuing the Israelites, the Israelites cross safely. At Pluto's instigation, they fall into various sins and provoke God's wrath against themselves. The Law is promulgated; manna rains down; a cloud by day and fire by night point out the way through the wilderness, in which they wandered for forty years because of their sins. Three thousand people are slain for idolatry; the tabernacle is erected, and the high priest's garments are described. Korah and his companions murmur and conspire against Moses; fiery serpents are sent. Moses dies on Pisgah, and the people cross the Jordan under Joshua's leadership. The land of Canaan is described, where various wars take place between the people of Jerusalem and the inhabitants of the land. At last Joshua emerges victorious and subdues the Canaanites; after his death come the Judges, who deliver the people of Jerusalem when they are repeatedly oppressed by enemies through Pluto's envy. Gideon puts the enemies to flight by a stratagem. Jephthah, returning home victorious, sacrifices his daughter. The blessedness of the Church is described, and all these narratives are applied to Christ.

Vide Genebra. Chron. lib. I.
marginalia.text_en: The Israelites remained two years beside Mount Sinai and the neighbouring places; in which time Moses built the Tabernacle and published the Laws. In Kadesh-Barnea they stayed nineteen years; another nineteen years they wore away, now advancing, now falling back, now straying; until through forty-two encampments or stations they came, after forty years, to the eastern bank of Jordan. See Genebrard. Chron. lib. I.

marginalia.text: Ob aeris salubritatem coelique temperiem, & soli ubertatem prae omnibus aliis mundi regionibus celebris est haec terra apud Scriptores tam sacros quàm profanos. Vide Deut. 8. Plin. Joseph, &c.
marginalia.text_en: For the healthfulness of its air, the mildness of its sky, and the richness of its soil, this land is celebrated above all other regions of the world by writers sacred as well as profane. See Deut. 8. Plin. Joseph, &c.

marginalia.text: Virgilius Portam dixit; ut: porta tonat coeli, aërem intelligens: ego portas, propter tres aëris regiones, quae liberantur nubibus & caligine, aestivo calore & luce.
marginalia.text_en: Virgil said "gate" in the singular—as in "the gate of heaven thunders"—meaning the air; I say "gates" on account of the three regions of the air, which are freed from clouds and darkness by summer heat and light.
marginalia.explanation: He justifies departing from Virgil's singular by the three-region physics of the air.

marginalia.text: Candidus auratis aperit cum cornibus annum Taurus; inquit Virgilius. Ego Solem in Tauro nomino, cui cornua tribuo propter radios: tum quod forma arietina sub nomine Jovis Ammonis colebatur, teste Macrob. Sat. lib. I. cap. 21. tum quod idem est Sol qui Bacchus, qui cornibus pingebatur.
marginalia.text_en: "The white Bull with gilded horns opens the year," says Virgil. I name the Sun in Taurus, and assign him horns on account of his rays: both because he was worshipped in the form of a ram under the name of Jupiter Ammon, on the testimony of Macrob. Sat. lib. I. cap. 21, and because the Sun is the same as Bacchus, who was painted with horns.

marginalia.text_en: Not every use of horses was forbidden to the Hebrews, as some would have it, but excessive luxury, in horses as much as in wives, in gold and silver, and the rest: that is, lest they should place their trust in a multitude of horses, as the nations do, having forsaken the true God; lest they should have commerce with the Egyptians, among whom the finest horses were; lest they should grow proud at the number of their horses.
marginalia.explanation: He is disputing the common reading of the Mosaic prohibition on horses.

marginalia.text_en: By these tropes and figurative expressions I describe the Church and spiritual graces, a mode once familiar to the holy Prophets: "The mountains," Isaiah says, "will sing; the trees will clap; in place of the wild nard a fir will rise, and in place of the nettle a myrtle will grow," ch. 55.

prose.la: Juvenis Sampson dum uxorem peteret, leonem in viâ occidit, in cujus cadavere inter redeundum alvearium repperit. Hic Judex factus, Philistarum frumentum incendit, qui suasu Plutonis in eum conspirant, & ligant; ille autem ruptis vinculis, mille hostes Asini maxillâ sternit, & portas Gazæ aufert; postea blanditiis Dalilæ allectus, illi robur suum prodidit, & capillos amisit; & sic in hostium potestatem devenit, qui oculis effossis, in pistrinum dant. Dum verò postea Dagonis sacra peragunt, Sampsonem in templum ludibrii gratiâ introduci jubent, qui columnæ totis viribus (quæ jam cùm capillis creverant) incumbens, templum diruit, hostesque omnes & seipsum illa ruina obruit. Dagonis solemnitas describitur; Eli, qui Sampsoni successit, audita clade Israëlitarum & filiorum morte, subito expirat; sequitur Samuel, qui Saulum in Regem ungit, petente populo: Saulus filium habuit Jonathan, Davidi charissimum, qui Philistas in fugam conjecit: David autem Goliah Philistærum ducem, qui ipsum ad monomachiam provocaverat, lapillo sternit, & hostes fugat; postea Saulus Davidem veritus regnum affectare insensus servat, & necare statuit, sed frustra; semper enim incolumis evasit; interea Saulus sollicitus de belli eventu inter ipsum & Philistas, consulit Sagam, quæ ostendit illi Samuelis spectrum, ex quo didicit se ipsum cum filiis in prælio casurum; quod sequenti die contigit. David autem solus regno potitus, hostes undique domuit, multas urbes deditione cœpit: sed domesticis seditionibus vexatus est, præcipuè Absalonis, quem Joab occidit. Senio tandem confectus rex, Salomonem successorem designat, qui Templum, cujus magnificentia hic describitur, condidit, & pacem coluit; quæ omnia in Christum quadrant.
prose.en: When the young Samson was going to seek a wife, he killed a lion on the way and, as he returned, found a beehive in its carcass. After being made judge, he burned the Philistines' grain; at Pluto's prompting they conspired against him and bound him. Breaking his bonds, however, he struck down a thousand enemies with an ass's jawbone and carried off the gates of Gaza. Afterwards, enticed by Delilah's blandishments, he revealed his strength to her and lost his hair; thus he fell into the power of his enemies, who gouged out his eyes and consigned him to the mill. Later, while they were performing Dagon's rites, they ordered Samson to be brought into the temple for their amusement. Bracing himself with all his strength against a column—his strength having now grown again with his hair—he brought down the temple and buried all his enemies and himself beneath its ruins. The festival of Dagon is described. Eli, who succeeded Samson, suddenly expired upon hearing of Israel's defeat and the death of his sons. Samuel followed him and, at the people's request, anointed Saul king. Saul had a son, Jonathan, who was very dear to David and put the Philistines to flight. David, meanwhile, struck down with a small stone Goliath, the Philistines' leader, who had challenged him to single combat, and routed the enemy. Afterwards Saul, fearing that David aspired to the throne, kept him under hostile watch and resolved to kill him, but in vain, for David always escaped unharmed. Meanwhile Saul, anxious about the outcome of the war between himself and the Philistines, consulted a witch. She showed him the apparition of Samuel, from whom he learned that he and his sons would fall in battle; this happened the following day. David then gained sole possession of the kingdom, subdued his enemies on every side, and captured many cities through their surrender. Yet he was troubled by rebellions at home, especially Absalom's, which Joab ended by killing him. At last the king, worn out by old age, designated Solomon as his successor. Solomon built the Temple, whose magnificence is described here, and cultivated peace. All these things correspond to Christ.

Hills and mountains were called arces (citadels) from arcere, to keep off — or from the Arcadians, because under Evander they held the best-fortified hills.

Domus autem Regis, domus saltus Libani, & domus Reginae, non fuerunt tria aedificia, sed unum in tres partes distinctum, ut probat Pineda de rebus Salom. lib. 5. cap. 5. Hic loca erant designata ad jus dicendum, ad convivia, ad arma custodienda: basilica erat magna & pulchra, &c. quam ad causas forenses agitandas, & lites decernendas condidit, &c. In ejus medio aedes quadrata, &c. in ea tribunal magnificum, ubi Rex jura reddebat. Joseph. antiq. lib. 8. cap. 2.
marginalia.text_en: That the King's house was joined to the Temple is inferred from verse 9 of 1 Kings 7, where it extends as far as the greater, or outer, court of the Temple. The King's house, the house of the forest of Lebanon, and the Queen's house, however, were not three buildings, but one building divided into three parts, as Pineda proves in De rebus Salom., book 5, chapter 5. Here places were appointed for administering justice, holding banquets, and storing arms. The basilica was large and beautiful, etc.; he founded it for conducting legal proceedings and deciding disputes, etc. In its midst was a square hall, etc., and in that hall a magnificent tribunal where the King administered justice. Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 2.
marginalia.explanation: He is arguing, with Pineda and Josephus, that the three "houses" of Solomon were one complex adjoining the Temple.

marginalia.text: Ad majorem magnificentiam probabile est, Salomonem habuisse omnia vestium genera, quae res Aegyptia byssus vel sericus bombyx suppeditare, aut Tyrus, Sydon, Seres, aliaeque provinciae peregrinae exhibere potuerunt.
marginalia.text_en: For greater magnificence, it is probable that Solomon possessed every kind of garment that Egyptian resources, whether fine linen or silk, could supply, or that Tyre, Sidon, the Seres, and other foreign lands could furnish.

marginalia.text: Laena vestis genus, quo Flamines uti solebant inter sacrificandum. Cicer. de claris orat. Chlamys autem vestis militaris pallio brevior; ipse agmine Pallas in medio chlamyde, & pictis conspectus in armis. Virgil. Aeneid. 8.
marginalia.text_en: The laena is a kind of garment that the Flamens customarily wore while sacrificing. Cicero, On Famous Orators. The chlamys, by contrast, is a military garment shorter than the pallium: "Pallas himself, in the midst of the column, conspicuous in his chlamys and decorated armor." Virgil, Aeneid 8.

marginalia.text: Ob vestes pictas & variegatas olim celebres fuere Babylon & Aegyptus. Haec ibi Memphitis tellus dat munera; victa est pectine Niliaco jam Babylonis acus. Martial.
marginalia.text_en: For painted and variegated garments Babylon and Egypt were once famous. "Here the land of Memphis gives these gifts; Babylon's needle has now been beaten by the Nile's comb." Martial.

marginalia.text: Cum tot uxores & concubinas habuerit, Aegyptias, Tyrias, Sidonas, luxui & lautis vestibus conficiendis intentas: sine dubio delicatissimas illi vestes suppeditarunt.
marginalia.text_en: Since he had so many wives and concubines — Egyptian, Tyrian, Sidonian — intent upon luxury and upon the making of costly clothes, they doubtless supplied him with the most exquisite garments.

marginalia.text: Tharsi & Ophir sunt diversae regiones, illa in Africa, haec in India: ex illa Psittaci, Simiae, dentes Elephantini, argentum delata Salomoni, ex hac aurum, ligna pretiosa, & gemmae: de Tharsi & illius divitiis vide 1. Reg. 10. 22. & 2. Paralip. 9. 21. de Ophir verò 1. Reg. 10. 11. 2. Chron. 9. 10.
marginalia.text_en: Tharshish and Ophir are different regions, the one in Africa, the other in India: from the former parrots, apes, elephants' tusks and silver were brought to Solomon; from the latter gold, precious woods and gems. On Tharshish and its riches see 1. Reg. 10. 22. & 2. Paralip. 9. 21.; on Ophir, 1. Reg. 10. 11. 2. Chron. 9. 10.

marginalia.text: Κανδάκην αἰθίοπες πᾶσαν τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως μητέρα καλοῦσι
marginalia.text_en: That this was the common name of the queens in the island of Meroe, Pliny asserts, lib. 6. cap. 29. It is probable that the queens of the Ethiopians were called by this name: Strabo lib. 17. relates the war of Petronius with Candace, the one-eyed queen of the Ethiopians; of another Candace we read in the Acts of the Apostles, cap. 8. "The Ethiopians call every mother of the king Candace," as the Greek scholia have it. By Ethiopia here I understand the Arabian Ethiopia, which is also called the region of Sabaea, and India: for all who dwell on this side of the river Indus are called Indians by Curtius, lib. 9.
marginalia.explanation: He treats Candace as a royal title, not a personal name.

marginalia.text: Tanta hic fuit thuris & aromatum abundantia, ut pro sarmentis & caetera ignis faciendi materia, cinnamomo, cassia, caeterisque utuntur. Strabo l. 16.
marginalia.text_en: So great was the abundance of frankincense and spices here that, in place of brushwood and other fuel, they use cinnamon, cassia, and the like. Strabo, book 16.

prose.la: Regina Saba Judæam ingressa, Oratores Solymam cum muneribus ad Salomonem mittit: qui cognita ex iis adventus Reginæ causa, ut nempe sapientiam suam audiret, & aulæ magnificentiam videret; Reginæ cum ingenti pompâ obviam fit, quam benigne hospitio excepit, eique aulæ suæ splendorem, & urbis varia monumenta ostendit: illa autem admirata tantam sapientiam & gloriam, domum revertitur: Regnum Salomonis cum Christi regno comparatur: Christiani ad pacem inter se, & bellum cum Turca exstimulantur. Salomone mortuo, regnum ipsius dividitur sub filio Roboam; & Solymam expugnat Rex Aegypti. Abias filius Roboami, Jeroboam bello vicit; Abiæ verò filius Asa, Aethiopes superavit. Jehosophat cum Achab à Syriis superatur, classis quam in Indiam missurus erat, submersa est. Precibus hostes devicit. Jehoram Idololatra fratres occidit; Achasiam Jebu peremit; Athalia regnum invadit; Achasiæ, Amasiæ, Vzziæ, Jothami, Achasi, Ezechiæ, Manassæ, Josiæ, Joasi, Joacimi, Joacin, & Sedechiæ vitæ breviter describuntur. Judith Holofernem somno vivoque obrutum, obtruncat, & patriam obsessam liberat. Chaldæi Solymam expugnant, & funditus cum Templo evertunt: Judæi autem captivi Babylonem ducuntur, ubi 70 annos manserunt; quo tempore Prophetas Deus ad illos misit, qui de Christo liberatore vaticinantur.
prose.en: The Queen of Sheba, having entered Judaea, sends envoys with gifts to Solomon at Jerusalem. Learning from them the cause of the Queen's coming — namely, that she might hear his wisdom and see the magnificence of his court — he goes out to meet her with great pomp, receives her kindly as his guest, and shows her the splendour of his court and the various monuments of the city; and she, marvelling at such wisdom and glory, returns home. Solomon's kingdom is compared with the kingdom of Christ, and Christians are spurred on to peace among themselves and to war against the Turk. Solomon being dead, his kingdom is divided under his son Rehoboam, and the king of Egypt storms Jerusalem. Abijah, Rehoboam's son, defeated Jeroboam in war; and Abijah's son Asa overcame the Ethiopians. Jehoshaphat, together with Ahab, is defeated by the Syrians, and the fleet he was about to send to India was sunk; by his prayers he overcame the enemy. Jehoram the idolater kills his brothers; Jehu makes away with Ahaziah; Athaliah seizes the kingdom. The lives of Ahaziah, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah, Joash, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah are briefly set out. Judith beheads Holofernes, overwhelmed by sleep while yet alive, and delivers her besieged country. The Chaldaeans storm Jerusalem and overthrow it utterly along with the Temple; the Jews are led captive to Babylon, where they remained seventy years, during which time God sent to them the Prophets, who prophesy of Christ the deliverer.

marginalia.text: Per Dianam exercentem choros in jugis Cynthi Lunam intelligo inter minora sidera vagantem : tantae altitudinis fuit Cynthus mons, ut Sol & Luna degentibus in imis vallibus viderentur verticem contingere, & in eo movere: hinc orta est fabula de partu Latonae. Hanc ob causam stellas Oreades voco, quod videantur intuentibus è profundis vallibus in montibus degere: erat ergo regina inter comites, velut inter stellas Luna minores.
marginalia.text_en: By Diana leading the dances on the ridges of Cynthus I understand the Moon wandering among the lesser stars. Mount Cynthus was of such height that to those living in the valleys below, the Sun and Moon seemed to touch its summit and to move upon it; whence arose the fable of Latona's childbearing. For this reason I call the stars Oreads, because to those gazing up from the deep valleys they seem to dwell upon the mountains. The queen, then, was among her attendants as the Moon among the lesser stars.
marginalia.explanation: He is unpacking the mythological simile of his own verse.

marginalia.text: Salomonem Soli orienti comparo. Lycia & Xanthus orientales sunt respectu insulae Delos, invisit Delum cum tenebris occulta, luce suâ manifestat; ἀπὸ τοῦ δῆλος. Illi & Lunae sagittas tribuunt Poëtae propter radios, Soli autem laurum, ob hujus arboris innatum calorem, aurum verò propter aureum Solis colorem in ortu. Cretes, Dryopes, Agathyrsi, aliaeque gentes, Solem orientem adorarunt, illique festa & tripudia consecrarunt.
marginalia.text_en: I compare Solomon to the rising Sun. Lycia and the Xanthus lie eastward with respect to the island of Delos; he visits Delos when it is hidden in darkness and makes it manifest by his own light—from δῆλος, "manifest." The poets attribute arrows to him and to the Moon because of their rays; to the Sun they attribute the laurel because of the heat innate in this tree, and gold because of the Sun's golden colour at its rising. The Cretans, the Dryopes, the Agathyrsi, and other nations worshipped the rising Sun and consecrated festivals and dances to him.

marginalia.text: Molech seu Melech, Regem significat. Rex autem fuit Saturnus: ex genere etiam sacrificiorum colligitur, quod Saturnus idem fuit qui Molech; nam pueri immolabantur, & tympana pulsabantur, in Saturni sacris: qui mos duravit usque ad proconsulatum Tiberii. Vide Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 9.
marginalia.text_en: Molech, or Melech, signifies King. Now Saturn was a king; and from the kind of sacrifices too it is gathered that Saturn was the same as Molech, for boys were sacrificed and drums beaten in the rites of Saturn — a custom which lasted down to the proconsulship of Tiberius. See Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 9.
marginalia.explanation: He is identifying the biblical Molech with the pagan Saturn on the evidence of child sacrifice.

marginalia.text_en: In 2 Chronicles 24 he is called Baal; this was the god of the Phoenicians, whom they call Beelsamen, that is, lord of heaven; the Greeks, however, call him Jove. Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 1.7. Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17, bears witness that all the gods are traced back to the Sun.

marginalia.text: Hic Joacimus tradidit se obsessum Nabuchadnozari sub finem regni sui anni tertii, vel initium quarti: datis obsidibus (inter quos Daniel & tres pueri) & parte vasorum templi. Dan.1. tributarius in regno suo relinquitur: sed deficiens ad Aegypti Regem à Babyloniis iterum captus est, & an. 11. regni moritur.
marginalia.text_en: This Jehoiakim surrendered himself to Nebuchadnezzar when besieged, at the end of the third year of his reign or the beginning of the fourth, after hostages had been given—among them Daniel and the three youths—together with part of the Temple vessels. Dan. 1. He was left in his kingdom as a tributary; but after defecting to the king of Egypt, he was captured a second time by the Babylonians and died in the eleventh year of his reign.
marginalia.explanation: He is fixing the chronology of Jehoiakim's two submissions.

marginalia.text: Hic Joacin, seu Jechonias, regni mense tertio cum matre se Chaldaeis dedidit, & cum totâ sobole Babylonem ductus, initium dedit captivitati 70 annorum.
marginalia.text_en: This Jehoiachin, or Jechonias, surrendered himself, together with his mother, to the Chaldaeans in the third month of his reign and, being taken to Babylon with his entire family, inaugurated the seventy-year captivity.

marginalia.text: Zedechia fuit filius Josiae, patruus Jechoniae, 2. Reg. cap.24. at phrasi Hebraeâ frater dicitur, 2. Chron. 36. 10.
marginalia.text_en: Zedekiah was the son of Josiah and the uncle of Jechonias, 2. Reg. cap. 24; but by a Hebrew idiom he is called his brother, 2. Chron. 36. 10.
marginalia.explanation: He reconciles the apparent disagreement between Kings and Chronicles by appeal to Hebrew usage.

marginalia.text: Hic Genebrardum sequor, qui ad tempus Nabuchadnozar hanc historiam refert. Ann. regni 13, misit Holofernem in Judaeam & Samariam. An. verò 19. reliquias Judaeorum Babylonem transtulit. Antea quoque dispersi erant Judaei sub Sennacherib, de quâ dispersione loquitur Achior cap. 5. libri Judith: & fortasse Isaias cap. 1. Alii hanc historiam ad Cambysis vel Assueri tempora referunt, sed nunquam erant Persarum Reges Nabuchadnozar vocati. Genebr. Chron. lib. 2.
marginalia.text_en: Here I follow Genebrard, who refers this history to the time of Nebuchadnezzar. In the thirteenth year of his reign he sent Holofernes into Judaea and Samaria; in the nineteenth he removed the remnant of the Jews to Babylon. Earlier too the Jews had been scattered under Sennacherib, and it is of that dispersion that Achior speaks in cap. 5 of the book of Judith, and perhaps Isaiah in cap. 1. Others refer this history to the times of Cambyses or Ahasuerus; but the kings of the Persians were never called Nebuchadnezzar. Genebr. Chron. lib. 2.
marginalia.explanation: He adopts Genebrard's dating of the book of Judith and rejects the rival Persian chronology.

prose.la: Exactis 70 annis captivitatis Babylonicæ, & concessa Judæis in patriam redeundi venia, rursus extruitur Templum cum urbe, frustra moras injiciente Satana; & quamvis Judæi tempore captivitatis, & post reditum domum, partim domesticis dissidiis, partim, ab extremis hostibus in extremum discrimen sæpe adducti sunt: Deus tamen memor cœlestis Solymæ seu Ecclesiæ, varios populi sui desensores & vindices excitavit: nempe Hester, Alexandrum Macedonem, Ptolomæum Philadelphum, Mathiam, cum filiis Juda, Jonathan, Simone Hircano, qui typi fuerunt Christi cœlestis Solymæ propugnatoris: sed cùm Deus provocatus esset sceleribus Aristobuli regis & successorum ejus, permisit Judæam in Romanorum potestatem venire: Babylonis namque imperium jam Romam translatum fuit, ubi variis Pluto afficitur honoribus, ejusque regnum longe lateque propagatur: Solyma in servitutem redacta, extincta Macchabæorum familia, & Davidis stirpe sublata, Idumæis regibus subjicitur Judæa: interea Christus tam diu exspectatus & toties promissus, ex Spiritu Sancto concipitur, nunciante Angelo: variisque prodigiis antecedentibus, nascitur ex Maria Virgine. Digressio fit in laudes Christi: ostenditurque illum esse solum Deum Judæorum & Gentium: Græcorum vanitas in multiplicandis diis arguitur: Judæi ut Christum Ducem & Pastorem agnoscant, admonentur atque exhortantur.
prose.en: After the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity had elapsed and the Jews had been granted permission to return to their homeland, the Temple was rebuilt together with the city, while Satan tried in vain to cause delays. And although the Jews, both during the captivity and after their return home, were often brought into extreme peril, partly by domestic dissensions and partly by external enemies, God nevertheless, mindful of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the Church, raised up various defenders and champions of his people: namely Esther, Alexander the Macedonian, Ptolemy Philadelphus, Mattathias with his sons Judas, Jonathan, and Simon Hyrcanus, who were types of Christ, the champion of the heavenly Jerusalem. But when God had been provoked by the crimes of King Aristobulus and his successors, he permitted Judaea to fall under Roman power; for the empire of Babylon had by then been transferred to Rome, where Pluto is accorded various honours and his kingdom is spread far and wide. With Jerusalem reduced to servitude, the family of the Maccabees extinguished, and the line of David removed, Judaea was subjected to Idumaean kings. Meanwhile Christ, so long awaited and so often promised, was conceived by the Holy Spirit at the angel's annunciation and, after various portents had preceded his birth, was born of the Virgin Mary. A digression is made in praise of Christ, and he is shown to be the sole God of the Jews and the Gentiles. The vanity of the Greeks in multiplying gods is condemned; the Jews are admonished and exhorted to acknowledge Christ as their Leader and Shepherd.

marginalia.text: Per Lunam intelligo Romanum imperium; per sidera, minora regna Romae subdita; per agnam, multitudinem populorum; per manes, obscuras & barbaras gentes, nunc ad Christum praedicatione Evangelii tanquam incantamento conversas; sed Judaei sunt adhuc aspides surdae, duriores lapidibus, quibus Sanctum Stephanum incantatorem suum lapidaverunt, nec audiverunt vocem incantantis. Augustin. in Psal. 57. Tunc Luna caelo deducta est, cùm Roma de summo honoris gradu & dominatu deturbata est, ob caedes & crudelitatem in Christianos. Hac phrasi utitur Cicero 6. Philip. collegam de caelo detraxisti.
marginalia.text_en: By the Moon I understand the Roman empire; by the stars, the lesser kingdoms subject to Rome; by the ewe-lamb, the multitude of the peoples; by the shades, the dark and barbarous nations, now converted to Christ by the preaching of the Gospel as if by an incantation. But the Jews are still deaf asps, harder than the stones with which they stoned Saint Stephen, their own charmer, and they did not hear the voice of the one charming. Augustine on Psalm 57. The Moon was drawn down from heaven at the time when Rome was thrown down from the highest degree of honour and dominion, on account of her slaughters and her cruelty against the Christians. Cicero uses this expression in the 6th Philippic: you have dragged your colleague down from heaven.
marginalia.explanation: A full allegorical key to the passage, with Augustine on the deaf asp and Cicero adduced for the idiom of drawing down from heaven.

marginalia.text: Christus Deum soboles, id est, Regum, qui Dii vocantur.
marginalia.text_en: Christ the offspring of gods, that is, of Kings, who are called gods.
marginalia.explanation: Justifies the Virgilian phrase deum soboles by taking the gods to be kings, so called in Scripture.

marginalia.text: Christus Patris incrementum dicitur, non active, sed passive: non crevit Pater additione Filii, sed Filius crevit qua homo in sapientia, gratia, statura, virtutibus, & gloria: Deus opt. max. est vere Jupiter, quia vere juvans Pater. ὁ τῶν ἁπάντων Ζεὺς πατὴρ ὀλύμπιος; Sophocles. Sic Salustius. Du Bartas Deum verum Neptunum vocat: qui vray Neptune, &c.
marginalia.text_en: Christ is called the increase of the Father not actively but passively: the Father did not grow by the addition of the Son, but the Son grew, as man, in wisdom, grace, stature, virtues, and glory. God, best and greatest, is truly Jupiter, because truly a helping Father. "Zeus, Olympian father of all things" — Sophocles. So too Sallust. Du Bartas calls the true God Neptune: qui vray Neptune, &c.
marginalia.explanation: Defends applying the Virgilian magnum Iovis incrementum and the pagan divine names to Christ, with the etymology Jupiter = juvans pater.

prose.la: Hoc Libro continentur vaticinia de Christi nativitate, vitâ, miraculis, morte, resurrectione, ascensione, &c. deque amplitudine, potentiâ, & splendore coelestis Solymæ, id est, Ecclesiæ & Regni Christi. Ubi arreptâ occasione sit digressio in laudes Regum Jacobi & Caroli nutritiorum Ecclesiæ parentum. Ubi etiam invehitur Virgilius in sacrilegos Solymæ expilatores, qui rapaci hoc sæculo, Ecclesiæ bona, furore nefario perciti, uncis manibus diripuerunt.
prose.en: This book contains prophecies concerning Christ's nativity, life, miracles, death, resurrection, ascension, and so forth, and concerning the greatness, power, and splendour of the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, of the Church and kingdom of Christ. Here, occasion being taken, a digression is made in praise of Kings James and Charles, the nursing fathers of the Church. Here too Virgil inveighs against the sacrilegious plunderers of Jerusalem, who in this rapacious age, driven by an impious frenzy, have torn away the Church's goods with grasping hands.
