marginalia.text: Lucretius, Virgilius, aliique Poetae, supremum Deum aethera vocant; & quem Plato à cursu Θεὸν, hunc Aristoteles à sempiterno cursu αἰθέρα nominavit, non autem ab ardore, ut Cicero. Hic igitur Christo non attribuo cum Marcionitis aetherium corpus, sed aetherium Patrem cum Ecclesia.
marginalia.text_en: Lucretius, Virgil and other poets call the supreme God "aether"; and him whom Plato named Θεός from running, Aristotle named αἰθήρ from everlasting running — not from burning, as Cicero did. Here, therefore, I do not attribute to Christ an ethereal body, as the Marcionites do, but an ethereal Father, as the Church does.
marginalia.explanation: He guards a pagan epithet for God against the charge of Marcionite heresy about Christ's body.

prose.la: Christi nativitatem Angeli pastoribus nunciant, qui ut jussi Bethlemum ad puerum contendunt; octavo die Christus circumciditur. Interea nova Stella Magos ex Persia Hierosolymam ducit: Herodes autem ex rumore novi Regis nati turbatus, pueros Bethlemiticos per satellites occidit, Josephus verò & Magi in somno ab Angelo moniti, fugerunt; ille cum puero & matre in Ægyptum; hi per aliam viam in patriam. Postquam Christum adorâssent, Simeon eum Sacerdoti oblatum ulnis amplexus est. Duodecimum agens annum inter Doctores in templo à parentibus inventus fuit, cum quibus privatam vitam egit, donec anno ætatis suæ exacto trigesimo, à Johanne baptisatus in Jordane fuit. Johannis solitaria & frugalis vivendi ratio commendatur. Christum jejunantem variis tentationibus invadit Pluto ; quo victo & fugato, domino ministerium suum praebuerunt Angeli; duodecim tenuis fortunæ socios elegit Christus: describitur conditio Regni Christi: bellum inter Christianos detestatur Poëta, & varias intexit divinas & pias meditationes.
prose.en: The angels announce Christ's birth to the shepherds, who, as commanded, hasten to Bethlehem to the child; on the eighth day Christ is circumcised. Meanwhile a new star leads the Magi from Persia to Jerusalem. Herod, however, disturbed by the report that a new king has been born, kills the children of Bethlehem through his henchmen. Joseph and the Magi, meanwhile, warned in a dream by an angel, fled: the former with the child and his mother into Egypt, the latter by another road to their homeland. After the Magi had worshipped Christ, Simeon embraced him in his arms when he was presented to the priest. In his twelfth year he was found by his parents among the teachers in the temple, and with his parents he lived a private life until, upon completing the thirtieth year of his life, he was baptized by John in the Jordan. John's solitary and frugal manner of life is commended. Pluto assails the fasting Christ with various temptations; after Pluto has been defeated and driven away, the angels offer their service to the Lord. Christ chooses twelve companions of modest means; the character of Christ's kingdom is described; the poet condemns war among Christians and interweaves various divine and pious meditations.

prose.la: Postquam 12 ministros in unum convocasset Christus, variis documentis & præceptis instruit, adversus hostium malitiam animat: describitur Divini Verbi potentiâ in ore Apostolorum, quo regnum Plutonis corruit. Christus in nuptiis Cana Galilææ aquam in vinum vertit; postea flagello mercatores è Templo ejecit; Evangelium prædicat, & omnes morborum species curat. Cum Samaritana ad puteum Divinum colloquium habet; cùm autem undique confluentes turbæ illum premerent, Petri naviculam ascendit, & ex ea populum docuit, doctrinam verò miranda piscium captura confirmavit: viduæ unicum filium defunctum resuscitat. Dum verò in navi dormiret, excitatâ tempestate Pluto illum cum sociis submergere tentat; sed è somno experrectus, objurgatis ventis procellam sedat. Ex duobus Gadarenis juvenibus Dæmones ejecit, qui porcorum gregem aquis immerserunt. Hæmorrhoissam contactu vestis sanat. Filiam Jairi mortuam vivificat. Magdalenam lachrymantem à Dæmonibus liberat. Reguli filium absens sanat. In Patria docens, in vitæ discrimen adducitur: Baptista incarceratur, & decollatur. Describitur Herodis convivium, & res gestæ Herodis magni obiter decantantur.
prose.en: Having summoned the twelve ministers together, Christ instructs them with various teachings and precepts and emboldens them against the malice of their enemies. The power of the Divine Word in the mouths of the Apostles is described, through which Pluto's kingdom collapses. At the wedding in Cana of Galilee, Christ turns water into wine; afterward he drives the merchants from the Temple with a whip; he preaches the Gospel and cures every kind of disease. He has a divine conversation with the Samaritan woman at the well; but when crowds converging from every direction pressed upon him, he boarded Peter's little boat and taught the people from it, confirming his teaching by a wondrous catch of fish. He raises a widow's only son from the dead. While he was sleeping in the boat, however, with a storm stirred up, Pluto tried to drown him together with his companions; but Christ, awakened from sleep, rebuked the winds and calmed the tempest. He cast demons out of two young Gadarenes; the demons plunged a herd of swine into the waters. Through contact with his garment he heals the woman with an issue of blood. He restores Jairus's dead daughter to life. He frees the weeping Magdalene from demons. From a distance he heals the ruler's son. While teaching in his own country, he is placed in mortal danger; the Baptist is imprisoned and beheaded. Herod's banquet is described, and the deeds of Herod the Great are celebrated in passing.

notes.text: Per Centauros, semiviros & semiequos, intelligo homines belluinis voluptatibus, caedibus, rapinis, & ebrietati deditos. Per Scyllaeas biformes, quarum una filia Nysi patriae & patris proditrix: altera, Phorcicum Neptuno in adulterio deprehensa, intelligo parricidas, proditores, & adulteros. Briareus qui Jovem coelo detrudere conatus est, signat seditiosos, qui Superis, qui superioribus potestatibus resistunt: Hydra bellua Lernae, indomitam & rebellem multitudinem: Chymaera, idololatriam ethnicam, & cultum daemonum, cujus tres erant partes; Caput leoninum flammivomum significans terrores rudi populo injectos, & crudeles victimas pecudum & hominum: 2. venter caprinus, promiscuas & infandas libidines notans: 3. cauda anguinea, venenatam de Deo doctrinam, & vafram eorum politiam indicans. Hanc Bellerophon, scilicet Christus, βελνφόρος, Evangelii Pegaso (est enim πηγὴ ἀιὲν ὦν fons perennis, & omni Pegaso velocius) interemit. Gorgones pulchro quondam capillitio, postea anguineo, & aspectu truculento, denotant voluptatum illecebras, quae primâ specie videntur pulchrae, at brevi homines cruciant quasi veneno infectos, & in saxa mutant. Has non Persius Jovis, sed Christus Jovae filius: non Minervae scuto, & Mercurii gladio, sed sua ipsius sapientia & eloquentia in praedicatione Evangelii superavit. Harpyiae, divites avaros notant, qui semper sordidi, famelici, & rapaces sunt. Pallent ore, quia curis assiduis torquentur. Alatae & celeres sunt ad rapiendum, uncis manibus ad retinendum; sub virgineo vultu, id est, sub specie honestatis avaritiam sordidam tegunt. Hos praedicatio Evangelii, & operatio miraculorum, velut Calais & Lethes Aquilonis alati filii abegerunt. Geryon autem triceps, notat triplicem Satanae potestatem in animas, corpora, & fortunas hominum: Christus verus Alcides hunc sustulit, & omnes praedictas pestes virtute suâ pedibus subjecit.

marginalia.text: βεληφόρος
marginalia.text_en: By the Centaurs, half men and half horses, I understand men given over to brutish pleasures, slaughter, plunder, and drunkenness. By the two-formed Scyllas—of whom one was the daughter of Nisus, betrayer of her country and her father, and the other the daughter of Phorcys, caught in adultery with Neptune—I understand parricides, traitors, and adulterers. Briareus, who attempted to drive Jupiter from heaven, signifies seditious men, who resist the gods above, who resist the higher powers. The Hydra, the beast of Lerna, signifies an untamable and rebellious multitude. The Chimaera signifies heathen idolatry and the worship of demons, which had three parts: first, the flame-spewing lion's head, signifying the terrors inflicted upon an untaught people and the cruel sacrifices of beasts and human beings; second, the goat's belly, marking promiscuous and unspeakable lusts; third, the serpent's tail, indicating their poisoned doctrine concerning God and their crafty statecraft. Bellerophon—that is, Christ, the missile-bearer—slew this monster with the Pegasus of the Gospel (for the Gospel is an ever-flowing spring and swifter than any Pegasus). The Gorgons, whose hair was once beautiful but later serpentine, and whose appearance was grim, denote the allurements of pleasures, which at first sight appear beautiful but soon torture men as though they had been poisoned and turn them into stones. These were overcome not by Persius—that is, Perseus—son of Jupiter, but by Christ, the son of Jehovah; not with Minerva's shield and Mercury's sword, but through his own wisdom and eloquence in the preaching of the Gospel. The Harpies signify the greedy rich, who are always squalid, famished, and rapacious. Their faces are pale because they are tormented by unremitting cares. They are winged and swift to seize, and have hooked hands to hold fast; beneath a maiden's face—that is, under an appearance of honesty—they conceal sordid avarice. The preaching of the Gospel and the working of miracles drove these men away, just as Calais and Lethes—that is, Zetes—the winged sons of the North Wind drove away the Harpies. Three-headed Geryon, moreover, signifies Satan's threefold power over men's souls, bodies, and fortunes: Christ, the true Hercules, destroyed him and by his own power placed all the aforesaid plagues beneath his feet.
marginalia.explanation: A systematic key turning Virgil's monsters at the mouth of the underworld into an allegory of vice, idolatry and Satan's power, with Christ as Bellerophon, Perseus and Hercules.

marginalia.text: His vocabulis non fictitias Deas marinas, sed pisces intelligo. Cymodocia à fluctibus; Melite à Mellite, Sapore; Galataea, à colore lacteo nomen habent. Thetis Νηρηῒς Ωκεάνης maris filia ab Homero vocatur, quod Pisces in mari generentur. Hym. in Apoll. Doto inter piscium genera recensetur ab Hygino, lib. Fab.
marginalia.text_en: By these terms I understand not fictitious sea-goddesses but fish. Cymodocia takes her name from the waves; Melite from a honeyed flavor; and Galatea from a milky color. Thetis is called by Homer Νηρηῒς Ωκεάνης, "a daughter of the sea," because fish are born in the sea (Hymn to Apollo). Doto is numbered among the kinds of fish by Hyginus in his book of Fables.
marginalia.explanation: He deflects the charge of putting pagan sea-deities into a gospel poem by construing the Nereids' names as names of fish.

prose.la: Christus auditâ Johannis nece, ex Galilæâ in desertum secessit, ubi populi turbam ingentem miraculose pavit: Super mare ambulat, & Petrum pene immersum, liberat: Populum docet & sanat; motus Chananitidis precibus, & fide filiam ipsius sanitati restituit. 38 annos morbo laborantem ad Bethesdam quendam, ad valetudinem reduxit: & hydropicum curat. Pharisæi invidia moti, satellites quosdam miserunt ad capiendum Christum, qui ipsi verbis Christi capti, re infectâ, redierunt: Postea à furente plebe saxis impetitur. In monte Thabor transfiguratur: descendens a monte, puerum à Daemone liberat; & Apostolos objurgat. Capernaum ingressus, tributum solvit, pecunia in ore piscis reperta. Dum docet in Templo, iterum lapidatur, sed se subduxit & Bethaniam pervenit, ubi Lazarum suscitat jam mor¬
prose.en: When Christ had heard of John's murder, he withdrew from Galilee into the wilderness, where he miraculously fed a vast crowd of people. He walks upon the sea and rescues Peter as he was all but sunk. He teaches and heals the people; moved by the prayers and the faith of the Canaanite woman, he restores her daughter to health. He brought back to health a man at Bethesda who had laboured under his disease for thirty-eight years, and he cures a man with dropsy. The Pharisees, stirred by envy, sent certain officers to seize Christ; but they, themselves taken captive by Christ's words, returned with nothing done. Afterwards he is assailed with stones by a raging populace. On Mount Tabor he is transfigured; coming down from the mountain, he frees a boy from a demon and rebukes the Apostles. Having entered Capernaum, he pays the tribute with the money found in a fish's mouth. While he teaches in the Temple he is stoned again, but withdrew himself and came to Bethany, where he raises Lazarus, already dead—

prose.la: Finita cœna, Christus cum Apostolis in hortum Gethsemani secessit, ubi precantem & sanguine sudantem, Angelus solatur; exhibetque poculum lethali vino plenum, quod ipse Pater cœlestis miscuit: Poëticè describitur poculum ab Angelis fabricatum; in cujus oris, Christi, Apostolorum, multorumque Christianorum martyria cælantur: Describitur Christi passio in horto, quem Judas ibidem, comitante sceleratorum militum cohorte, osculo prodidit, verùm omnes ad Christi vocem in terram ceciderunt; tandem
prose.en: Supper ended, Christ withdrew with the Apostles into the garden of Gethsemane, where, as he prayed and sweated blood, an Angel consoles him, and holds out to him a cup filled with deadly wine, which the heavenly Father himself had mixed. The cup, wrought by the Angels, is described in the poetic manner; upon its rim are chased the martyrdoms of Christ, of the Apostles, and of many Christians. prose.la: Christus cruci affixus inter duos fures elevatur; titulus superscribitur: alter latronum ridet, alter Christum fatetur & orat, cui Paradisus promittitur. Dumque Christus pro inimicis orat, matrem graviter dolentem conspicit, eamque Johanni commendat. Describitur miraculosa Solis Eclypsis, & Judæorum cæcitas; tandem Dominus dolores innumeros & non dicendos passus, exspiravit; tremit terra, rumpuntur saxa, sepulchra recluduntur: velum Templi, quod hic describitur, discerptum est. Centurio his prodigiis motus, Christum Dei Filium agnoscit; dumque latronum crura franguntur, lancea Christi latus confoditur, ex quo sanguis & aqua fluxit. Describitur Christi descensus ad inferos, & ejusdem sepultura; nec non Josephi, Nicodemi, & Matrum pietas; Virginisque Mariæ acerbissimi dolores. Christus tertiâ die, territis custodibus terræ motu, resurrexit. Angeli mulieribus, illæ Apostolis resurrectionem nunciant. Petrus & Johannes ad sepulchrum currunt. Vigiles autem pecunia corrupti, mendacium spargunt, Discipulos nempe Dominum furto abstulisse: Judæorum malitia in Christum describitur. Magdalena adstat sepulchro plorans,
prose.en: Christ, fastened to the cross, is raised up between two thieves; the title is written above him. One of the robbers mocks, the other confesses Christ and prays, and to him Paradise is promised. And while Christ prays for his enemies, he catches sight of his mother in heavy grief and commends her to John. The miraculous eclipse of the Sun is described, and the blindness of the Jews; at last the Lord, having suffered pains beyond number and beyond telling, breathed his last: the earth quakes, the rocks are split, the tombs are laid open, and the veil of the Temple — which is here described — was rent apart. The Centurion, moved by these prodigies, acknowledges Christ to be the Son of God; and while the thieves' legs are broken, Christ's side is pierced by a lance, out of which flowed blood and water. Christ's descent to the underworld is described, and his burial; likewise the piety of Joseph, of Nicodemus, and of the Mothers, and the most bitter sorrows of the Virgin Mary. On the third day Christ rose again, the guards struck with terror by the earthquake. The Angels announce the resurrection to the women, and they to the Apostles; Peter and John run to the sepulchre. But the watchmen, corrupted with money, spread the lie that the Disciples had carried off the Lord by theft. The malice of the Jews against Christ is described. Magdalene stands weeping at the sepulchre,

marginalia.text: Hic non intelligo poëticas Nymphas, quae cum quercubus nasci & interire fingebantur, ideo ἁμαδρυάδες dictae; sed rusticanas virgines ad Christi fidem conversas. Δρῦς Quercum, vel Arborem significat: illae autem inter arbores versantur. Ob hanc rationem Gallorum Magi sunt dicti Druidae.
marginalia.text_en: Here I do not mean the Nymphs of the poets, who were feigned to be born and to perish together with their oaks, and were for that reason called Hamadryads, but country maidens converted to the faith of Christ. Δρῦς signifies an oak, or a tree; and these women live among the trees. For this same reason the wise men of the Gauls were called Druids.
marginalia.explanation: He explains why nymphs may stand for rustic Christian women, glossing the Greek root shared by Hamadryad and Druid.

prose.la: Christus in cœlum ascensurus, varia præcepta dat Apostolis, quibus benedicit, & Petro Ecclesiæ suæ curam credit. Deus Pater convocato Angelorum concilio, de Christi Filii in cœlos elevatione mentem suam aperit, cui Angeli ascenserunt omnes, & Christo ascendenti ministerium præbuerunt. Poëticè sub formâ magnifici Palatii describitur cœlestis gloria. Dum verò Apostoli Christum ascendentem, oculorum acie curiosius sequuntur, à duobus Angelis de ipsius reditu docentur. Describitur ultimum judicium, & Christi redeuntis gloria: Interea Apostoli Hierosolymam redeunt, ubi in superiore cœnaculo dum unanimes orationi incumbunt, Spiritus Sanctus specie ignitarum linguarum in eos descendit. Hic varia mysteria, & meditationes interseruntur. Christiani ad pacem mutuam rursus exhortantur, & ad bellum Turcis inferendum.
prose.en: Christ, about to ascend into heaven, gives various instructions to the Apostles, blesses them, and entrusts the care of his Church to Peter. God the Father, having summoned a council of the Angels, reveals his purpose concerning the elevation of Christ his Son into the heavens; to this all the Angels assented, and they rendered their service to Christ as he ascended. The glory of heaven is poetically described under the figure of a magnificent palace. While the Apostles, however, follow the ascending Christ rather too intently with their gaze, two Angels instruct them concerning his return. The Last Judgement and the glory of Christ's return are described. Meanwhile the Apostles return to Jerusalem, where, as they devote themselves with one accord to prayer in the upper room, the Holy Spirit descends upon them in the form of fiery tongues. Various mysteries and meditations are interwoven here. Christians are again exhorted to mutual peace and to wage war against the Turks.

marginalia.text: Hic per Astra Titania non intelligo Solem, de quo in sequenti versu, sed minores Stellas: & sic (puto) intelligendus est Virgilium Aen. lib. 6. cùm ait, Spiritum alere Titania astra, id est, Solem fovere luce suâ Stellas. Est enim Sol anima & mens mundi, ut Macrobius ostendit ex Poëtis & Philosophis. Soli nomina omnium Deorum conveniunt. Sol etiam Spiritus à Salomone vocatur, Eccles 17. Falluntur ergo Virgilii Interpretes (si ipse non fallor) qui per Astra Titania Solem intelligunt.
marginalia.text_en: Here, by "the Titanian stars," I do not understand the Sun, which is mentioned in the following verse, but the lesser stars; and this, I think, is how Virgil should be understood in Aeneid 6, when he says that the Spirit nourishes the Titanian stars—that is, that the Sun sustains the stars with its own light. For the Sun is the soul and mind of the world, as Macrobius shows from the poets and philosophers. The names of all the gods belong to the Sun. The Sun is also called Spirit by Solomon, Ecclesiastes 1.7. Virgil's commentators are therefore mistaken—unless I am mistaken myself—when they understand "the Titanian stars" to mean the Sun.
marginalia.explanation: He is openly correcting the standard commentators on Aeneid 6 over the phrase Titania astra.

marginalia.text: Deus est ubique, sedes tamen ejus in Oriente locatur, et in loco honoratiore: Ergo Christus qui Oriens ab alto dicitur, Luc. 1. in Oriente collocatur; illinc Christum rediturum speramus. In Oriente pedes Christi steterunt, Zach. 14. nempe in monte Olivarum. Ex Oriente, scilicet ex Paradiso ejecti sumus; ad Orientem oramus: Orientem Templa nostra respiciunt. Vide Justinum Martyr. ad Orthodox. q. 118. Tertull. in Apolog. Origin. Homil. 5. in Num. Athanas. de Necess. quaest. q. 14. Basil. de Spir. Sanct. cap. 27. &c. Et 70 Interpretes, ad Orientem, Psal. 68. 36. Sicut fulgur exit ab Oriente, sic erit adventus Filii hominis, Matth. 24. 27.
marginalia.text_en: God is everywhere, yet his seat is placed in the East, and in the more honourable place. Therefore Christ, who is called the Dayspring from on high, Luke 1, is placed in the East; and from thence we hope that Christ will return. In the East the feet of Christ stood, Zach. 14 — namely, on the Mount of Olives. Out of the East, that is, out of Paradise, we were cast forth; toward the East we pray; our churches look toward the East. See Justin Martyr ad Orthodox. q. 118. Tertull. in Apolog. Origen Homil. 5. in Num. Athanas. de Necess. quaest. q. 14. Basil. de Spir. Sanct. cap. 27. &c. And the Seventy Interpreters, "toward the East," Psal. 68. 36. "As the lightning cometh out of the East, so shall the coming of the Son of man be," Matth. 24. 27.

notes.text: Jupiter quasi juvans Pater, seu potius Jovae Pater, à voce Jehova, ut Adonis ab Adonai. Sapientiores Ethnici eundem supremum agnoverunt Deum, quem nos: hunc Jovem nominarunt, cujus nos progenies sumus: ut ex Arato probat D. Paulus. Nec minus licet nobis hunc appellare Jovem quàm Θεόν, aut νοῦν, aut λόγον, aut πνεῦμα: quae voces sunt Ethnicae. Ζεὺς πρῶτος γίνετο, Ζεὺς ὕστατος ἀρχικέραυνος, &c. Vide Orphei Carmen de Jove.

marginalia.text: Vitta ornabantur olim Sepulchra, Cadavera, Sacerdotes, victimae mulieres, Sponsae, Athletae, Victores, Principes, &c. His Vitta pro Diademate sumitur, nihil enim aliud fuit veterum Diadema, quam Vitta, Fascia, vel Taenia: haec namque indifferenter usurpari apud Authores video Diadema à διαδέω, revincio. Pompejus Diademate vulnus circumligavit: imposita capiti vincla veneranda gere. Sen. in Thyest. intelligit Diadema. * Paean Carmen est victoriae, ut ex Aeschylo docet Servius.
marginalia.text_en: Of old, tombs, corpses, priests, sacrificial victims, women, brides, athletes, victors, princes and the like were adorned with the fillet. Here the fillet is taken for the diadem, for the diadem of the ancients was nothing else than a fillet, band or ribbon: I find these words used indifferently by the authors. Diadema from διαδέω, I bind about. Pompey bound up a wound with his diadem. "Wear the venerable bands laid upon thy head": Seneca in the Thyestes means the diadem. * The paean is a song of victory, as Servius teaches out of Aeschylus.
marginalia.explanation: He justifies using vitta (fillet) where a royal crown is meant.

marginalia.text: Jupiter quasi juvans Pater, seu potius Jovae Pater, à voce Jehova, ut Adonis ab Adonai. Sapientiores Ethnici eundem supremum agnoverunt Deum, quem nos: hunc Jovem nominarunt, cujus nos progenies sumus: ut ex Arato probat D. Paulus. Nec minus licet nobis hunc appellare Jovem quàm Θεόν, aut νοῦν, aut λόγον, aut πνεῦμα: quae voces sunt Ethnicae. Ζεὺς πρῶτος γίνετο, Ζεὺς ὕστατος ἀρχικέραυνος, &c. Vide Orphei Carmen de Jove.
marginalia.text_en: Jupiter, as it were "helping Father," or rather "Jova-Father," from the word Jehovah, as Adonis from Adonai. The wiser pagans acknowledged the same supreme God as we do; they named him Jove, "whose offspring we are," as St Paul proves from Aratus. Nor is it any less lawful for us to call him Jove than God (θεόν), mind (νοῦν), word (λόγον), or spirit (πνεῦμα), which are pagan words. "Zeus came into being first, Zeus last, ruler of the thunderbolt," and so forth. See Orpheus's poem on Jove.
marginalia.explanation: The central defence of the cento's method: pagan divine names are admissible for the true God.

Ambros. in Psal. 118. serm. 5.

marginalia.text: O bonorum equorum duodeca-jugum mirabile, quibus fraena pacis, habenae sunt charitatis constricti inter se concordiae vinculis, & jugo fidei subjecti: quatuor rotis Evangelii mysterium totius orbis finibus invehentes, bonum aurigam portantes Dei verbum, cujus flagello fugatae sunt illecebrae saeculares, &c. Ambros. in Psal. 118. serm. 5.
marginalia.text_en: O wonderful twelve-horse team of good horses, whose bits are peace and whose reins are charity, bound fast to one another by the bonds of concord and set under the yoke of faith; who upon four wheels carry the mystery of the Gospel to the ends of the whole earth, bearing a good charioteer, the Word of God, by whose whip the enticements of the world are put to flight, &c. Ambros. in Psal. 118. serm. 5.
marginalia.explanation: The twelve horses are the apostles and the four wheels the evangelists.
